So the redrive never knew that key, and a bridge's original attempt that committed without the bridge hearing back (a lost response) was redriven into a second command. `POST /v1/parked-deliveries` now takes an optional top-level `idempotencyKey` (`command_trigger` only, reserved prefixes refused), stored in the row's `request` as `idempotencyKey`; the redrive runs under `(token client_id, that key)`, exactly the original submission's identity, and falls back to the per-row key only without one. Each bridge derives the header and the report field from one `inbound_idempotency_key` function, so they can't disagree. Test: `retrying_a_parked_trigger_whose_original_attempt_committed_is_deduplicated` (real REST trigger with a key commits, the same key is parked, the retry is deduplicated; 2 commands with the redrive ignoring the stored key, 1 with it) and `skilj-kafka`'s `a_parked_trigger_message_reports_the_idempotency_key_it_was_sent_with`. What remains uncovered: an `ExternalEvent` original attempt that committed without a `dedupe` cursor. Nothing identifies it, and a bridge that wants redelivery safety sends a cursor anyway (all three do when the broker provides a position).

Visible change: a redriven `CrossContextRoute` command's `client_id` is now `cross-context-route`, not `parked-delivery-retry`. It is the route's command either way, and the key only dedupes under the route's own client id.

Tests: `concurrent_retries_of_one_parked_delivery_redrive_it_once` (`skilj/tests/parked_deliveries_graphql.rs`, failed with 2 events before the fix, stable over 5 runs after), and the redrive in `a_persistently_failing_target_parks_instead_of_blocking_forever` now goes through `parked_delivery_redrive_identity` and asserts that a second redrive is `Deduplicated`.

<a id="test-harness-cleanup"></a>
## 66. Test harness: the embedded Postgres (and broker containers) never stopped

`/tmp` - a 7.7G RAM-backed tmpfs on the WSL dev machine - hit 100% during a session of three full `cargo test --workspace` runs, taking the Kafka broker tests down with admin-operation timeouts and making even shell output fail with `ENOSPC`. The cause: 46 test files each started their own `postgresql_embedded` server and kept it in a `static` `OnceCell`. Rust never drops statics, so `PostgreSQL`'s `Drop` (stop the server, delete the temp data dir) never ran. Every run left about one live Postgres per test binary plus its data dir behind: 128 orphaned servers (1,100+ processes) and 297 `/tmp/.tmp*` dirs by the time it was noticed. It had been happening since the first embedded-Postgres test. This is very likely what was behind this project's repeated mid-session WSL crashes: memory pressure from tmpfs plus hundreds of idle postmasters, not anything in skilj itself. The bridge crates' Kafka/Artemis/NATS testcontainers had the identical leak for the identical reason (a `ContainerAsync` in a `static`).

**Fix: a new, unpublished `skilj-test-support` crate.** `database_url(name)` returns a database of the calling test binary's own on `DATABASE_URL`'s server - see §166 and §167 - or, with no `DATABASE_URL`, a database on the process's one embedded server. On first start it spawns a watchdog `sh` in its own process group. The watchdog polls `kill -0` on the test process and, once that process is gone, runs `pg_ctl stop -m immediate` and deletes the data dir and the password file's own temp dir. That dir is only deleted when it really is a `.tmp*` dir under the temp dir: `postgresql_embedded` falls back to the current directory if it can't make one, and deleting that would delete the checkout. `remove_container_on_exit(id)` does the same for a container (`docker rm -f -v`). A watchdog process rather than an exit hook, because the exits that caused the pile-up (Ctrl-C, killed binaries, VM crashes) run no exit hooks. Its own process group so a terminal's Ctrl-C doesn't kill it along with the tests.

Each test file keeps its own connect/migrate logic (they differ: pool sizes, whether a `Pool` or a URL is kept, `connect_and_migrate` vs inline); only the ~20-line start-a-server block and the `_embedded` field went. 42 files converted mechanically by script, 4 by hand.

**Verified**: a SIGINT and a SIGKILL to a process holding an embedded database both leave no server and no temp dir within a few seconds, and a full `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` leaves 0 Postgres processes, 0 `/tmp/.tmp*` dirs and 0 containers afterwards (before the fix it left ~40 servers, several GB of `/tmp` and 3 containers per run). 937 tests pass, no skipped Postgres tests.

`cargo publish` strips a dev-dependency with a `path` and no `version` (checked with `cargo package -p skilj-core`: the packaged manifest has no `skilj-test-support`), so none of the published crates gain a dependency on the unpublished one. The cost: tests in a downloaded `.crate` tarball no longer build on their own, which nothing here relies on.

<a id="ci-silent-skip-guard"></a>
## 67. CI's silent-skip guard never fired

`.woodpecker.yml` greps the test log for Postgres `skipping: ...` notes and fails the build if any appear (commits `67960be`/`d3281ab`), so a CI run can't go green without touching the database. It ran `cargo test --workspace` without `--nocapture`. The note is printed from inside a test that then returns early and *passes*, and libtest discards a passing test's captured output, so the note never reached the log. Reproduced by pointing `DATABASE_URL` at a dead port: all 59 `persistence.rs` tests skipped and "passed", `cargo test` exited 0, and the CI grep matched nothing. The earlier verification used a hand-inserted log line, which can't show a capture problem.

Fix: CI runs `cargo test --workspace -- --nocapture`, and the grep drops its `^` anchor, since parallel tests can interleave a note mid-line after another test's `test ... ` prefix. Checked both ways: the dead-port reproduction now matches, and a healthy full run (119 KB of output) matches nothing. The same capture effect had hidden the Docker-down broker skips locally too. They show up under `--nocapture` (`skilj-kafka`/`-amqp`/`-nats` tests "passing" in 0.01s is the other tell).

<a id="projection-type-collision"></a>
## 68. Colliding or invalid projection type names in `ProjectionQuery`

Each registered projection gets a GraphQL type named `{bounded_context}_{projection}` (`projection_types::graphql_type_name`), with nested shapes and enums named `{parent}_{field}`. Two problems, both silent:

- **Collisions.** Bounded context names may contain `_`, so `a_b` + `c` and `a` + `b_c` both produce `a_b_c`; a nested `{parent}_{field}` can also equal another projection's top-level name. `async_graphql`'s dynamic `SchemaBuilder::register` keeps only the *last* type per name, with no error (checked directly), and the `projection` resolver tags every result with `graphql_type_name(bc, name)`. So both projections were served, one of them rendered through the other's type: wrong or missing fields, no error. No access-control impact, since each query still checks its own bounded context first.
- **Invalid names.** Projection names and state field keys aren't validated as GraphQL names. `finish()` accepts `order-summary` or a serde-renamed `total-amount` field without complaint, but the published schema is then not valid GraphQL, which breaks clients that parse it (codegen, GraphiQL, fragments). Separately, `total_amount` and `totalAmount` both become field `totalAmount` and overwrite each other the same silent way.

Fix, in line with how this module already treats an unparseable projection schema (exclude it and log why, rather than fail the whole schema): `build` claims each projection's generated names all-or-nothing (`admit_type_names`). A projection whose names are invalid or already taken is excluded with a `tracing::warn!`. A state field without a valid, unique GraphQL name is left out (before any nested type gets named after it). The admitted `(bounded_context, projection)` pairs go into the schema as `AdmittedProjections` data, and `projection` / `projectionUpdates` refuse anything outside it with `projection_not_in_schema`. That set is keyed by the pair, not the type name, because a colliding pair shares the name. This module's two `eprintln!` warnings became `tracing::warn!`, matching the crate's "emit via `tracing` only" rule stated in `schema.rs`.

Tests: `colliding_projection_type_names_serve_one_and_refuse_the_other` (`skilj/tests/projection_query.rs`; both served before, exactly one after, and the shared type carries only the served projection's field) plus unit tests for the name grammar, all-or-nothing admission and field skipping.


<a id="bounded-event-reads"></a>
## 69. Bounded event reads (`config.max_events_per_read`)

`GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/events/consume` and GraphQL `queryEvents` each served *every* matching event after their cursor, and loaded the whole remaining history into memory first to find them. A new consumer starting from the beginning of a long history, or one `GET /v1/events` without `after`, made the server load and serialize all of it in one response - enough to exhaust memory on either end.

**Spec.** `specs/skilj.allium` leaves paging to the wire contract, but *what* a rule serves is spec behaviour, so it now says so: a new `config.max_events_per_read` (default 1000) and a black-box `first_by_sequence(events, n)`. `FetchEvents`, `ConsumeEvents` and `QueryEvents` serve `first_by_sequence(<what they served before>, config.max_events_per_read)`. That keeps every rule's continuation exact: `ConsumeEvents`' auto-advance already moved the cursor to `highest_sequence(served)`, and a manual-ack caller acks the last event it handled, so a prefix is never skipped. The cap counts *served* events, not scanned candidates. A cap on candidates would leave a filtered consumer whose next N candidates all miss its filter with an empty page and an unmoved cursor forever. `CountEvents` stays unbounded - it is an aggregate, not a page. `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged (0 findings; 22 diagnostics, 5 findings as before).

**Implementation.**
- Pure functions keep their signatures (`fetch_events`, `consume_events`, `query_events` apply `DEFAULT_MAX_EVENTS_PER_READ`); `*_page` variants take the cap explicitly. `consume_events`' new-cursor seed moved into `initial_consume_position(token, history)`, a maximum, so it can be computed chunk by chunk; `consume_events_page` takes the resolved seed. `query_events_select` separates choosing a page from rendering it, since `skilj-graphql` resolves decryption keys asynchronously for just the served events.
- `db::for_each_event_chunk` walks a bounded context's history (optionally one event type) in chunks, cache-first per chunk with a `LIMIT`ed Postgres fallback (`list_events_from_limited`, `list_events_for_bounded_context_from_limited`). `db::collect_event_page` builds one page on it, calling the rule's own pure function per chunk, so the page is exactly the first N it would have served over the whole history. The chunk size is the page size, so memory stays at roughly one chunk plus one page, tuned by the one setting.
- `SkiljBuilder::max_events_per_read` (clamped to at least 1) reaches the REST state and `GraphqlState`. `skilj_rest::router` gained the parameter.
- `skilj-tui`'s query view shows how many events it has and loads the next page with `n`; it used to show one unbounded result. The Kafka/AMQP/NATS/Temporal bridges already poll consume in a loop and need no change. `skilj-inspector` reads Postgres directly and is unaffected.
- Not bounded at first: a tag-filtered `queryEvents` still loaded its tag-index matches whole before paging them - closed in §108.

**Breaking** for a `GET /v1/events` or `queryEvents` client that assumed one call returns everything: it must page (`after`=`nextCursor` / `afterSequence` = the last `sequence`) until a call returns nothing.

Tests: `reads_serve_bounded_pages_and_continue_where_they_stopped` (`skilj/tests/event_fetch_rest.rs`: page size 3 and a two-event cache window, so chunks come from both Postgres and the cache; `GET /v1/events` pages 7 events as 3+3+1 via `nextCursor`, a filtered page `[1,3,5]` fills across chunks, consume pages 3+3+1+0, and a `Latest` consumer minted after seven events seeds past all of them. Making the chunk walk stop after one chunk turns the filtered page into `[1,3]`) and `query_events_serves_bounded_pages_over_graphql` (`skilj/tests/graphql_business_surfaces.rs`, the bounded-context-wide path).


<a id="pageable-fetch-commands"></a>
## 70. Bounded, pageable `fetchCommands`

The command-side counterpart to §69, and the worse case of the two. `fetchCommands` loaded the bounded context's entire command history (`list_commands_for_bounded_context`, with no `ORDER BY`, so in whatever order Postgres returned rows), then made a database round trip per matching command to resolve decryption keys, then rendered all of them. It returned bare payload strings with no id or timestamp, so a client couldn't have paged even if it wanted to. §8's earlier decision to keep it a flat `[String!]!` was made when `Command` had no exposed id; that no longer holds.

**Spec.** `FetchCommands` (and the `CommandQuery` surface) gains an optional `after_command`, with the same bounded-context requirement `triggered_event` already has, and serves `first_by_recording(<candidates recorded after after_command>, config.max_events_per_read)`. The two new black boxes are `recorded_after(a, b)` and `first_by_recording(commands, n)`. `Command` has no sequence, but this library records commands in an order, and that is what pages follow. They don't follow `created_at`: two commands can share a timestamp, and a page boundary between them would skip or repeat one. The cap is the same `config.max_events_per_read` - despite its name it covers commands too, noted in the spec, rather than renaming a setting just added. `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged.

**Wire (breaking).** `fetchCommands(..., afterCommandId: String)` returns `[QueriedCommand!]!` `{ id, createdAt, payload }` instead of `[String!]!`. `id` is the command's own `Command.id`, and passing it back as `afterCommandId` gets the next page; there is no separate opaque cursor. An unknown `afterCommandId` is `Command_not_found` rather than a silent restart from the beginning. Within the workspace only tests called it.

**Implementation.** `db::command_recording_position` maps a command id to its `commands.id` key (a `BIGSERIAL`, so it only grows with insertion). `db::collect_command_page` walks commands after that position `ORDER BY id LIMIT <page size>`, a chunk at a time, calling the pure `event_store::fetch_commands_select` per chunk - the rule's filters and cap, now separate from rendering, the same split `query_events_select` got. Recording order isn't part of the domain `Command`, so the loader applies `recorded_after` and the ordering, and the pure function checks `after_command`'s bounded context (new `AfterCommandNotInBoundedContext`). Decryption keys are resolved for the served page only. `fetch_commands` keeps its signature (rendered strings, default cap) for existing callers.

Test: `fetch_commands_serves_bounded_pages_over_graphql` (page size 3: seven commands come back 3+3+1 in recording order via `afterCommandId`, each with `createdAt`; an unknown id is `Command_not_found`). The two existing `fetchCommands` assertions in the same file moved to the object shape.

<a id="bounded-history-reads"></a>
## 71. No request or background path loads a whole history any more

A sweep for the remaining callers of the full-history loaders after §69/§70 found five, none of them a paged read:

- **`countEvents`** loaded the whole bounded context to count it. The spec keeps `CountEvents` an unbounded aggregate, so only the loading changed: the rule's pure `count_events` runs per chunk (`db::for_each_event_chunk`) and the results are summed; a count is additive over disjoint chunks. The tag-filtered path still uses the tag index, as `queryEvents` does.
- **Both event subscriptions** (`allEvents`/`eventsByType`) loaded the full history from Postgres - uncached, on every subscribe and every reconnect - only to take its maximum sequence for the default starting point. Now `from_sequence ?? MAX(sequence)` via the existing `db::latest_sequence`, still after the broadcaster subscription so drift-audit finding #7's ordering holds.
- **`register_projection`'s history** (the `registerProjection` mutation, *every projection's reconciliation on every startup*, and template resync) was loaded whole for one question: does any event of a consumed type exist yet (does a new sync projection need a history fold)? `db::witness_events_of_types` answers it with at most one event per consumed type (`LIMIT 1`), which the pure function treats identically.
- **Catch-up ticks** for `CrossContextRoute`, `ScheduleDeadline` and `CancelDeadline` loaded every source event after their cursor per tick. A new one starting from the beginning of a long history would load all of it. Each tick now loads at most `MAX_EVENTS_PER_CATCH_UP_TICK` (1000). The cursor persists per processed event, so the next tick continues exactly where this one stopped. A new cursor's `Latest`/`AtTime` seed is one `MAX(sequence) ... WHERE event_type_name = $1 [AND metadata_created_at <= $2]` (`highest_sequence_of_type`), exact here because these seeds have no owner scope, unlike consume's.
- **`fold_history_into_new_sync_projection`** reads history in chunks of the same size; each event still commits in its own transaction.
- **Follow-up: async projection/rebuild and snapshot catch-up** (`catch_up_bounded_context`, `catch_up_snapshots`) loaded every event after the slowest projection's/snapshot's position, so a new async projection or a rebuild over a long history loaded all of it in one tick. Both now use the same `MAX_EVENTS_PER_CATCH_UP_TICK` cap - `caught_up_to` and snapshot progress persist per event, and a rebuild is only promoted once a re-read shows it at `latest`, so it simply promotes on the tick that finishes. The partitioned paths were already capped (`MAX_EVENTS_PER_PARTITION_TICK`). Test: `a_cold_start_catch_up_over_a_long_history_spans_ticks` (1003 events: tick one folds 1000, tick two the rest, final state identical).

Tests: `a_catch_up_tick_is_bounded_and_the_next_one_continues` (1003 source events against a 1000-event cache window: tick one routes exactly 1000 via the `LIMIT`ed Postgres path, tick two the last 3 from the cache, tick three nothing), and `query_events_serves_bounded_pages_over_graphql` now also checks `countEvents` = 7 across three 3-event chunks. The existing route/deadline start-position, subscription, templating, reconciliation and sync-projection suites all pass unchanged.

<a id="graphql-body-cap"></a>
## 72. Per-request bounds on `/graphql`

§69-§71 bounded what one *field* reads, but a GraphQL request could still route around them, and `/graphql` had no limits at all:

- **Body size, before authentication.** `async_graphql_axum::GraphQLRequest` reads the body as a raw stream - axum's default 2 MB body limit only applies to extractors that ask for it - and it runs before `graphql_handler`'s auth check. Its multipart path used `MultipartOptions::default()`, with no file-size or file-count limit, spilling parts to temp files (and this schema has no `Upload` type at all). Reproduced: an unauthenticated 3 MiB request was read whole and executed (HTTP 200).
- **Alias amplification.** `{ a1: queryEvents(...) a2: queryEvents(...) ... }` gives each alias its own `max_events_per_read` page, so one request multiplied the cap by the number of aliases; `countEvents` aliases each scan the whole history.
- **Depth and size.** No `limit_depth`/`limit_complexity`.

Fix, all configurable via `SkiljBuilder::graphql_limits(GraphqlLimits { .. })` (re-exported from `skilj`):
- `max_request_body_bytes` (default 2 MiB): a `POST /graphql` middleware reads at most that many bytes with `axum::body::to_bytes(body, max)` and answers `413` beyond it. Reading with a cap, rather than trusting `Content-Length`, also covers a missing or false header and chunked bodies. The extractor buffered the whole body anyway, so this adds no copy that wasn't there. The websocket upgrade (`GET`) is untouched.
- `max_depth` (24) and `max_complexity` (2000): `async_graphql`'s own validation limits. The dynamic schema API can't weight individual fields - every field counts 1 - which is why the next item exists.
- `max_expensive_fields` (10): an `async_graphql` extension on `parse_query` counts selections of `queryEvents`/`countEvents`/`fetchCommands`/`projection` per operation - aliases, inline fragments and each fragment spread included - and refuses the request with `query_too_expensive` beyond it. Only one operation executes, so the most expensive one decides. It runs before validation, which is what would reject a fragment cycle, so the walk doesn't follow one.

The defaults fit the standard full introspection query (graphql-js `getIntrospectionQuery`: depth about 14) that GraphiQL and codegen tools send; the test runs it.

Tests: `graphql_requests_are_bounded_in_size_depth_and_expensive_fields` (unauthenticated 3 MiB body gets 413, was 200 before; 20 `countEvents` aliases gets `query_too_expensive`; a 30-level-deep query is refused; full introspection passes), plus unit tests for alias/fragment counting, the most-expensive-operation rule, and a fragment cycle. Adding the tenth test to `skilj/tests/graphql_business_surfaces.rs` tipped it into §63's `PoolTimedOut` leak (every test leaks a `Skilj` with a 10-connection pool), so that file's setup now uses the same 4-connection pool its siblings do.

<a id="websocket-body-cap"></a>
## 73. The websocket endpoint shares the body cap

§72's body cap only covered `POST /graphql`. On the websocket (`GET /graphql` upgrade, subscriptions) every message is a GraphQL document too, and the connection accepts messages before - or without - a credential: a `connection_init` with no bearer resolves to no caller, which is allowed, since a subscription may need none. The upgrade used axum's defaults, 64 MiB per message and 16 MiB per frame. Reproduced: an unauthenticated connection sending a 3 MiB `subscribe` message had it parsed and executed (`next` with data). `graphql_ws_handler` now sets `max_message_size`/`max_frame_size` to `GraphqlLimits::max_request_body_bytes`, so one setting caps both transports; beyond it the connection is closed. Depth, complexity and the expensive-field budget already applied to subscription documents (same schema). Test: `an_oversized_websocket_message_closes_the_connection`.

How many subscriptions one authenticated connection may hold at once was left unbounded here; §74 closes that.

<a id="subscriptions-per-websocket"></a>
## 74. Subscriptions per websocket connection

Each subscription holds its own event-broadcast receiver and filters every committed event, so one connection opening thousands of them multiplied per-event work with no bound. No wrapping of `async_graphql`'s protocol handling was needed: `connection_init` inserts a per-connection `ConnectionSubscriptions` counter into the connection's data, and each subscription resolver (`allEvents`, `eventsByType`, `projectionUpdates`) claims a slot after its authorization checks - so a refused unauthenticated attempt never takes one - refusing with `too_many_subscriptions` once `GraphqlLimits::max_subscriptions_per_connection` (default 100) are running. The claim is a `SubscriptionSlot` guard owned by the subscription's stream, released on drop, so it goes however the stream ends: a client `complete`, the stream finishing, or the connection closing. Outside a websocket connection (a schema executed directly) there's no counter and no bound.

Wire note: `async_graphql` reports this resolver error as a `next` message carrying `errors`, followed by `complete` - not a protocol-level `error` message - the same as any other subscription resolver error.

Test: `a_connection_holds_at_most_max_subscriptions_at_once` (limit 2: two run, a third is refused, completing one lets a fourth start). With the guard's release removed, the fourth is refused and the test fails.

<a id="acknowledgements-serialized"></a>
## 75. Acknowledgements serialized with consume

`POST /v1/events/consume/ack` read the token's `ReadCursor`, checked `rule AcknowledgeEvents`' `sequence >= cursor.sequence` in Rust, and wrote the new position - three separate autocommit steps, outside the per-token advisory lock `GET /v1/events/consume` takes (§53). Two races followed:

- **Two acks** could both pass against the same old cursor, and the lower one could land last, moving the cursor *backwards* - violating the rule's own requirement and redelivering the events in between. Reproduced deterministically: a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger stalls the ack of 10 inside its write (Postgres takes the row lock before firing a `BEFORE` row trigger, so it holds the row). The ack of 5 meanwhile reads the still-uncommitted cursor (-1), passes, queues on the row, and then overwrites 10 with 5 - answered `200`. A first version of the test stalled the *lower* ack instead and passed without the fix, for exactly that row-lock reason, before being turned around.
- **An ack interleaving with a consume** could have the consume's claim (`checked_out_at`) written after the ack had cleared it, leaving a lease nobody holds and the next consumer served nothing until it expired.

Fix: the ack route runs in one transaction under `lock_read_cursor_for_consume`, with the cursor read inside it, exactly as consume does; `db::record_acknowledgement` now takes any executor. Test: `concurrent_acknowledgements_never_move_the_cursor_backwards` (the ack of 5 is now refused with `409 AcknowledgementRegresses` and the cursor stays at 10).

Manual-ack clients now acknowledge once per page (§69), which makes this path busier than it was.

<a id="reregistration-scheduler"></a>
## 76. Re-registration no longer rewinds the scheduler

`register_event_type`'s own comment says re-registration "leaves the position exactly where the scheduler left it" and that `last_fired_at` "is never touched". Under concurrency the implementation contradicted it. Registration builds its `EventType` from an unlocked `get_event_type` and `upsert_event_type` wrote *every* column on conflict, `schedule_position` and `last_fired_at` included. The scheduler advances those two under `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, so a scheduler firing between registration's read and its write was undone: the position rewound and the occurrence fired again. Every instance re-registers every type at startup, and a rolling deploy starts instances while others' schedulers run, so this is an ordinary window, not an exotic one. Reproduced deterministically: read the type, advance it the way the scheduler does, upsert the stale read - the position went back an hour.

Fix, in the upsert itself so every caller (the GraphQL mutation, startup reconciliation, template resync) gets it: on conflict `last_fired_at` is not written at all, and `schedule_position` takes the new value only `WHEN EXCLUDED.system_triggered_allowed AND NOT <current row>.system_triggered_allowed` - the pure function's own "scheduling newly enabled" test, evaluated against the row as it is now rather than the stale read. Test: `re_registration_never_rewinds_what_the_scheduler_advanced` (`skilj-core/tests/persistence.rs`), which also checks that opting in still sets the position. Two backlog tests in `skilj/tests/scheduled_events.rs` had simulated an outage by rewinding `schedule_position` through `upsert_event_type` - relying on exactly this behaviour. One then failed, and the `skip`-policy one kept passing only vacuously (no backlog at all). Both now set the position directly (`force_schedule_position`), as a stalled scheduler would leave it.

Checked and left alone: `upsert_projection` writes `caught_up_to` from the registration's copy the same way. A rewound `caught_up_to` only causes a rescan: the fold skips any event at or below a state row's own `as_of_sequence`, so nothing is folded twice, and registration legitimately sets `caught_up_to` after a new sync projection's history fold.

<a id="codegen-spec-validation"></a>
## 77. `skilj-codegen` validates a spec before emitting it

`generate` parsed a `.skilj.toml` (with `deny_unknown_fields`, so typos in *keys* were already caught) and emitted code straight from it, with no check on the *values*. Probed directly:

| Input | Before |
|---|---|
| type name `order-placed`, bounded context `Bad-Name` | **panic** in `build.rs` (`format_ident!` on a non-identifier) |
| field named `type` | `Error::Generated` - whose message says "a bug in skilj-codegen itself, not in your .skilj.toml" |
| duplicate type, duplicate field, an event and a command with the same name, a type named like the generated `<Context>Event` enum | "Ok", then a rustc error inside `$OUT_DIR` code |
| tag mapped to an undeclared field | "Ok", then `InvalidTagMapping` when the application registers types at startup |

Now `spec::validate` runs first and returns every problem at once as the new `Error::Invalid(Vec<String>)`. It checks the bounded context name against skilj-core's `valid_bounded_context_name` (mirrored, since this crate doesn't depend on skilj-core); type names as Rust identifiers and not keywords; field names as identifiers; duplicate fields; tags naming declared fields; and every generated name in one set (types, `…Payload` structs, the event enum, `decide_*` functions, `BOUNDED_CONTEXT`), since the marker types are unit structs sharing the value namespace. Keyword *field* names are supported rather than refused: JSON payloads use `type` routinely, and a raw identifier (`r#type`) is still named `type` by serde and schemars - checked by a test, since that's what makes the choice right; only `self`/`Self`/`super`/`crate`/`_`, which can't be raw, are refused. `Error::Generated`'s "a bug in skilj-codegen" wording is now true again.

Tests: four new ones in `skilj-codegen/tests/generate.rs` (every problem named in one error; a collision with the generated enum; `r#type` emitted with tag field `type`; `r#type` is `type` on the wire and in the schema). `skilj-demo`'s real `banking.skilj.toml` passes unchanged.

<a id="retry-backoff-panic"></a>
## 78. `RetryPolicy` backoff can't panic or collapse to zero

`RetryPolicy`'s fields are public and `next_backoff` runs inside long-lived background tasks (every `CrossContextRoute` catch-up and every bridge's retry loop), where a panic stops the task. Two ordinary-looking policies panicked inside `core::time`'s float-to-`Duration` conversion:
- `max_backoff: Duration::MAX`, a natural "no cap": once the backoff reached the cap, the cap round-tripped through `f64` no longer fitted back into a `Duration`.
- A negative `multiplier`: odd attempts produced a negative number of seconds.

`next_backoff` now treats a multiplier that isn't finite and non-negative as `1.0` (constant backoff), returns `max_backoff` itself once reached (never through `f64`), and converts with the non-panicking `try_from_secs_f64`. The result is always in `[0, max_backoff]`.

The four callers that store a due time rather than sleeping (the route's catch-up and the Kafka/AMQP/NATS outbound retry state) did `now + chrono::Duration::from_std(backoff).unwrap_or(zero)`. A backoff too large for chrono became a *zero* delay - retry immediately, forever, the opposite of backing off - and one that fitted could still overflow the addition, which panics in chrono. The new `RetryPolicy::next_attempt_at(now, attempt)` saturates at the latest representable instant instead, and all four use it; `skilj-retry` gains a `chrono` dependency for it (every crate that uses `skilj-retry` already depends on chrono). The inbound paths `tokio::time::sleep` on the `Duration`, which handles any value.

Tests: `skilj-retry/tests/backoff_edges.rs` (uncapped, negative and non-finite multipliers across attempts up to `u32::MAX` never panic and stay within the cap - the first two panicked before; `next_attempt_at` saturates rather than returning "now", and doesn't overflow near the end of time).

<a id="zero-sized-event-cache"></a>
## 79. A zero-sized event cache is off, not "everything is empty"

`EventCache::try_events_after` treats an existing but empty window as proof the bounded context has no events (true when the window can hold events: `freshen` has just caught it up). With `SkiljBuilder::event_cache_warm_up_count(0)` - the natural way to turn the cache off - every window was empty for a different reason: `freshen` loaded the *entire* history (the window knew no sequence, so it fetched from -1), pushed each event, and evicted each immediately. Every cache-backed read - `GET /v1/events`, consume, untagged `queryEvents`, the catch-up ticks - then silently returned **no events**, after loading the whole history for nothing. Reproduced: a zero-capacity cache reported a bounded context holding three events as empty.

Fix: a zero capacity is a disabled cache - `warm`/`append` do nothing and every lookup misses (`Ok(None)`), so callers read Postgres. Separately, `freshen` loaded everything since the window's last known sequence even when that was the whole history (a bounded context never warmed, such as one added at runtime) or more than the window can hold, only to keep the last `capacity`. It now refills such a window from the recent tail, with the same query `warm` uses, and fetches a delta only when it's smaller than the window.

Also from the same sweep of configuration values that reach tokio primitives: `event_broadcast_capacity(0)` panicked inside `tokio::sync::broadcast::channel` during `build()`; `EventBroadcaster::new` now clamps to 1. (`CommandBatcher`'s knobs already clamped; poll intervals only reach `tokio::time::sleep`, where zero is a busy loop, not a panic.)

Tests: `a_zero_capacity_cache_misses_instead_of_claiming_nothing_exists` (failed before), `a_cold_window_fills_from_the_recent_tail`, `a_zero_capacity_broadcaster_is_still_usable`.

<a id="plugin-panic-background-task"></a>
## 80. A panic in plugin code no longer ends a background task

Every background task `SkiljBuilder::build` spawns (async projection and snapshot catch-up, `CrossContextRoute`/`ScheduleDeadline`/`CancelDeadline` catch-up, deadline firing, the scheduler) is one detached `tokio::spawn` looping over a `for_each_concurrent` fan-out, and each unit of that fan-out runs application code: `Projection::project`, `Snapshot` folds, routes' and deadlines' mappings, deciders. Errors were handled per unit (logged, counted, retried next tick), but a *panic* - an `unwrap()` on a bad assumption in a projection - unwound out of `for_each_concurrent` and ended the task. For the async projection task that meant one buggy projection in one bounded context stopped async catch-up for **every** bounded context, permanently, with no signal beyond tokio's own panic message on stderr. Reproduced: a projection that panics in bounded context A, then an event in bounded context B - B's async projection never updated.

Fix: `contain_panic(task, unit, work)` wraps each unit (per bounded context, route, or deadline schedule) in `catch_unwind`. A panic is logged at `error` with the task, unit and panic message, and counted as `skilj.background_task.errors{task, reason="panicked"}`; the unit's open transaction rolls back when dropped during the unwind, so the next tick retries it, exactly like a unit that returned an error. A deterministic bug in one projection therefore panics once per tick in its own bounded context - loud, but contained - and nothing else is affected.

Checked and left alone:
- **The cross-instance listener** runs no application code (it refetches events and rebuilds the GraphQL schema from registered metadata), so it isn't wrapped.
- **The request path.** A decider or sync projection that panics while `CommandBatcher` is running a batch drops the batch's reply senders, so followers get a retryable `BatchFailed` rather than hanging, and `LeaderGuard` empties the queue on unwind so the next caller becomes leader (§59). The panicking request's own connection is dropped by the server; the process keeps running.
- **The Kafka/AMQP/NATS/Temporal bridges** run their own loops outside this crate and aren't covered here.

Test: `a_panicking_projection_does_not_stop_catch_up_for_other_bounded_contexts` (`skilj/tests/background_task_panics.rs`): a panicking async projection in one bounded context, then an event in another. The healthy projection never updated before the fix; after it, the broken projection panics every tick and the healthy one catches up.

<a id="jwt-audience-required"></a>
## 81. JWT audience is required

`verify_and_extract_subject` checked the signature, issuer, algorithm and expiry, but set `validate_aud = false`, and `IdpConfig` had no audience at all. The comment explained why: `jsonwebtoken::Validation::new` defaults to checking `aud` against an empty expected set, which rejected every real OIDC token (found against Dex in `skilj-helpdesk`), so the check was turned off rather than configured.

That left an audience-confusion hole. An IdP issues tokens to every application registered with it, all under the same `iss` and the same JWKS. With `aud` unchecked, a token issued to any other application at that IdP - a third-party app a user signed into, an internal tool, a compromised client - was a valid skilj credential for that user, and resolved to their skilj `Role` (step 3 of the spec's identity resolution note matches on the subject alone). The spec's "trusts the subject claim of a *verified* JWT" assumed verification established that the token was meant for this deployment. Reproduced: a validly signed token with `aud: "some-other-app"` was accepted.

Fix (breaking, chosen over an opt-in check so a deployment can't be left open by omission): `IdpConfig::new(jwks_endpoint, issuer, audience, signing_algorithm)`, plus `with_additional_audience` for a deployment reached through several client registrations. `IdpConfig::audiences` is never empty. Validation uses `set_audience(&audiences)` - a token passes if any of its `aud` values (string or array) matches any configured one - and adds `aud` to the required claims. Without that, `jsonwebtoken` skips the check for a token that has no `aud`, and such a token would still get through. The spec's two lists of IdP configuration values now include the expected audience (prose only; `allium check` unchanged).

Tests (`skilj-core/tests/jwt_verification.rs`): `verify_and_extract_subject_rejects_a_token_for_another_audience` (another app's `aud`, an array of only other apps, and no `aud`; fails against the old validation) and `verify_and_extract_subject_accepts_any_configured_audience` (the primary, an additional one, and an array containing ours). Every other test that mints a JWT now carries `aud`.

Also from this pass: `db::schema_ident` doubles an embedded `"` when quoting a bounded context name. No reachable path supplies one - names are validated at creation (`valid_bounded_context_name`), and resolvers check access, and so existence, before touching a per-context schema - but the function's doc comment calls the quoting defence in depth, and it wasn't without the escape. Unit test `schema_ident_quotes_and_escapes`.

<a id="bounded-http-requests"></a>
## 82. Every outbound HTTP request is bounded

Six `reqwest::Client::new()`s, none with a timeout - `reqwest` has no default one.

- **JWKS fetch** (`JwksCache`). `key_for` is single-flight (§65): the refetch runs while holding `last_refetch`. A JWKS endpoint that accepted the connection and never answered - a stalled proxy, a half-open connection after a network blip - held that lock forever. Every later lookup of an uncached `kid` queued behind it, so after the IdP's next key rotation no JWT could be verified until the process restarted. Any unauthenticated caller can trigger a refetch with a made-up `kid`, which is why `min_refetch_interval` exists, so it only takes one stall at the wrong time. Now each fetch carries `JwksCache::DEFAULT_FETCH_TIMEOUT` (10 s, `with_fetch_timeout` to override) and fails with `jwks_fetch_failed`, releasing the lock. Test: `a_stalled_jwks_endpoint_fails_the_fetch_instead_of_hanging` (an endpoint that never answers; the first lookup fails within the timeout and a second one answers immediately). Without the timeout it hangs past the test's 5 s bound.
- **Bridges** (`skilj-kafka`/`skilj-amqp`/`skilj-nats` `run_outbound`, `skilj_temporal::run`) built their own unbounded client, so one stuck request stalled that bridge's whole loop silently. Each crate now exports `http_client()` - `HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (30 s) end to end, 10 s to connect - which those loops use. `run_inbound` takes the caller's client, so its doc comment now asks for a bounded one and points at `http_client()`; the crates' own tests use it. A timeout is safe to retry: inbound calls carry an `Idempotency-Key` or a `dedupe` cursor (§39), and an outbound consume that was served but never answered is covered by the checkout lease (§53). Test in each crate: `a_stalled_skilj_fails_the_request_instead_of_hanging`.

Left alone: `skilj-tui`'s client. It's interactive and the user can quit it, so a stall there is visible and recoverable by hand.

<a id="cross-instance-connection-drop"></a>
## 83. A dropped cross-instance connection is noticed, not hidden

`cross_instance::Listener` wrapped `sqlx`'s `PgListener::recv`, which reconnects and re-`LISTEN`s on its own after a dropped connection (a Postgres restart or failover, an idle-connection reaper, a network blip) - transparently, so skilj never learned it happened. Every `NOTIFY` sent while it was down was lost. The module's doc comment said a missed message "just means the same self-heal path a same-process lagged receiver already takes (a fresh read)", but nothing did that read:

- **`RegistrationChanged` missed:** this instance kept its old GraphQL schema and template cache until some *later* registration change happened to reach it. An event type, projection or bounded context added on another instance meanwhile stayed missing here (`RegistrationReachesEveryInstance`), with no bound.
- **`EventAppended` missed:** live `allEvents`/`eventsByType` subscriptions on this instance silently skipped the events other instances committed in the gap. The spec (`DeliverySpansInstances`) calls a lost reach "a lateness", recovered by "the caller's own reconnect handoff" - but the connection stayed open, so the caller never reconnected. That's exactly the silent gap `DeliveryIsAtMostOnce` forbids and a local `Lagged` receiver already avoids by ending the stream.
- **`Revoked` missed:** a revoked subscription stayed open (the spec already accepted this as lateness).

Fix:
- `Listener::recv` uses `PgListener::try_recv`, which reports a lost connection as `Ok(None)` instead of hiding it. On that - or on any error - the listener reconnects and re-`LISTEN`s first, then returns the new `Message::Resync`. Re-listening before reporting matters: whatever the caller re-reads in response can't miss a change made after it. If reconnecting fails, `recv` returns the error and the next call tries again.
- The facade handles `Resync` like `RegistrationChanged` (schema rebuild, template-cache refresh), then calls the new `EventBroadcaster::signal_gap()`. That's a `watch` counter each subscription takes (`subscribe_gaps`) alongside its broadcast receiver, the same `select!` shape the revocation receiver already uses. The signal comes after the rebuild, so a client reconnecting in response finds the fresh schema.
- Event subscriptions end with `subscription_lagged` (the same code as a local lag, with a message naming the cause). `projectionUpdates` treats it as its own lag: refetch current state and carry on, since its contract is "current state", not "every event". Both paths re-check the caller's grant, which also covers a missed revocation.

The spec's two guarantees now say how the caller learns about the gap and when the schema catches up (prose only; `allium check` unchanged).

Tests, each in its own binary and database because they terminate every `LISTEN` backend: `a_dropped_connection_is_reported_as_resync_after_listening_again` (`skilj-core/tests/cross_instance_listener.rs`: terminate the listener's backend, `NOTIFY` while it's down, and `recv` returns `Resync` and then later notifications again. With the old transparent `recv` it waits forever for the lost one, failing at the 10 s bound) and `a_lost_listener_connection_ends_live_event_subscriptions` (`skilj/tests/cross_instance_resync.rs`: a live `allEvents` websocket subscription ends with `subscription_lagged` when its instance's listener connection is terminated; without `signal_gap` it carries on).

<a id="subscription-missed-span"></a>
## 84. Resuming a subscription delivers the missed span

The spec's handoff into the live feed - read state up to a sequence (`queryEvents`/`FetchEvents`/`QueryProjection`), then subscribe with that sequence as `fromSequence` - was described as gap-free, and it is the reconnect path every "subscription ended" signal points clients at (`subscription_lagged`, §83's gap, an ordinary disconnect). It wasn't gap-free. A subscription only receives events published to the broadcaster after it is created, and `fromSequence` merely filtered those (`from_sequence < event.sequence`). An event committed after the client's read but before its subscribe was in neither: not in the read, never delivered live. On a busy bounded context that window - a network round trip or two - is routinely non-empty. The spec model had the same hole (`DeliverToSubscriptions` fires only for events committed while a subscription exists), so the wording promised what neither the spec nor the code delivered. No test used `fromSequence` at all.

Fix, chosen with the user over "subscribe first, then read back and de-duplicate by sequence" (a merge duty on every client): the server fills the span. `resolve_start` runs after the broadcast receiver is taken, as the old default-start read did. It reads the latest committed sequence, and when `fromSequence` is below it, loads the events in `(fromSequence, latest]` - bounded context-wide for `allEvents`, the one type for `eventsByType` - with a `LIMIT` of `max_events_per_read + 1`. More than `max_events_per_read` refuses the subscription with `resume_span_too_large` rather than loading an unbounded span, and the caller reads it back first. Otherwise the stream delivers the span first and then the live feed, skipping live events at or below `latest`. Those were already in the span: the receiver predates the latest read, so they can arrive on it too. Committed order is sequence order within a bounded context (the per-context lock), so nothing below `latest` can commit after it was read. Span events go through exactly the live path (`deliver_one`, extracted from the two duplicated loop bodies): grant re-checked live, decrypt-on-read, private-field grants, filters and the `from_sequence` check. A subscription without `fromSequence` starts at the latest sequence and replays nothing, as before.

Spec: both creation rules gain `requires: <events after starting_point>.count <= config.max_events_per_read` (type-scoped for `CreateEventTypeSubscription`). `FreshEventsOnly`, `Subscription.from_sequence`, the note above the creation rules, the `DeliverToSubscriptions` note and the two reconnect passages now say the resume span is delivered, and that a read-back is only needed for a span longer than one read. `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged. The `subscription_lagged` messages now say to resubscribe from the last sequence received.

Test: `resuming_from_a_sequence_replays_the_missed_span_then_goes_live` (`skilj/tests/event_subscription.rs`, cap 3): four events, subscribe from the first, receive the other three in order, then a live one exactly once. `eventsByType` resumed from the third receives the fourth and the live one. A subscription from `-1` (five events) is refused with `resume_span_too_large`. With the span cleared, it times out waiting for the first replayed event.

<a id="subscription-select-before-read"></a>
## 85. Subscriptions select before they read the database

Each live event subscription handled every event committed in its bounded context the same way (`deliver_one`, §84, and the two loop bodies it replaced): re-fetch the caller's grant, resolve decrypt-on-read keys against it (more queries when the event type declares sensitive fields), read the context's private-field grants, and only then call `deliver_to_subscriptions`, which decides whether this subscription wants the event at all. For an `eventsByType` subscription, or an `allEvents` restricted to some types or filtered, most events fail that last step, so the database work was spent for nothing. The work is per subscription per event: `max_subscriptions_per_connection` (100) subscriptions on each of many connections, against a busy bounded context, is a steady multiple of the write rate in reads.

Fix: `event_store::subscription_selects(subscription, event)` - the part of the match that doesn't depend on the grant (bounded context, past `from_sequence`, one of the subscription's event types, its filters) - is now a pure function. `deliver_to_subscriptions` uses it followed by its grant status and owner-scope checks, so the two can't drift. `deliver_one` calls it before any query, so an event the subscription can't deliver costs no database access. Owner scope stays after the grant re-check: it depends on the grant's `scope`, which has to be the live one.

One consequence, checked and accepted: a grant revoked without the revocation push reaching this instance used to be noticed on the next event of *any* type in the bounded context (the grant re-check ran for all of them). Now it is noticed on the next event the subscription would deliver. Nothing leaks either way - delivery still re-checks the grant first - and the push itself (`RevocationClosesTheConnection`, drift audit finding #4) plus §83's resync on a lost cross-instance connection remain the ways a quiet subscription is closed.

Test: `subscription_selects_is_the_grant_free_part_of_delivery` (`skilj-core/tests/event_broadcast.rs`: another type and an event at `from_sequence` aren't selected and aren't delivered; a matching one is both; a revoked grant still selects but delivers nothing). The query saving itself isn't asserted by a test - Postgres' per-table statistics are flushed asynchronously, too loosely for a reliable count. The subscription suites pass unchanged.

<a id="parked-deliveries-pagination"></a>
## 86. Bounded, stable pages for `parkedDeliveries`

The last whole-table read on a request path after §69-§71: `parkedDeliveries(boundedContext:)` loaded every parked row in the bounded context, each with its full `request_json`, and returned them all. Parked rows accumulate exactly when something is persistently wrong - a bridge on a poison topic parks one per message - so the listing got heavier precisely when an operator needed it. It also wasn't in §72's expensive-field budget, so aliases multiplied it.

- **Bounded:** at most `max_events_per_read` rows per call (the same setting `fetchCommands` already reuses), continued with a new `after: String` argument.
- **Stable order:** `(first_failed_at DESC, id DESC)` - newest *parked* first - instead of `last_failed_at DESC`. A retry that fails again updates `last_failed_at` (the parked-row upsert), which would move a row across a page boundary mid-listing and skip or repeat it. `first_failed_at` never changes for a row. `id` breaks ties. New index `parked_deliveries_page_order` on exactly that order, created by `ensure_parked_deliveries_table` (now a `raw_sql` batch) on provisioning and every startup.
- **Deletion-safe cursor:** each `ParkedDelivery` has a new `cursor` field encoding its position (`{first_failed_at µs}:{id}`, `db::ParkedDeliveryCursor`) rather than naming the row, so retrying or discarding the last row of a page - the normal operator workflow while paging - doesn't invalidate the next page. A malformed cursor is `invalid_cursor`.
- `parkedDeliveries` joins `EXPENSIVE_FIELDS`.

`db::list_parked_deliveries` stays, unbounded, for tests and internal checks, now in the same order; the resolver uses `list_parked_deliveries_page`. `skilj-tui` reads the first page, which is now bounded.

Test: `parked_deliveries_are_served_in_bounded_stable_pages` (`skilj/tests/parked_deliveries_graphql.rs`, page size 2, five rows): pages come newest-parked first. Between pages, the last row served is discarded and the oldest row fails again (newest `lastFailedAt`). The remaining pages still yield exactly the other three in order, then empty. A bad cursor is refused. Before, one call returned all five. `legacy_parked_delivery_index_migrates_to_the_token_scoped_one` now expects the new index alongside the migrated ones.

<a id="idempotency-key-expiry"></a>
## 87. Idempotency keys expire (`idempotency_key_retention`)

`idempotency_keys` kept one row per accepted keyed submission forever - the spec said "Nothing expires" (§21's "no retention/TTL" precedent). Every bridge keys every inbound message (§64), as do `CrossContextRoute` deliveries, deadline firings and parked redrives, so the table grew with total traffic, unbounded. Flagged during this sweep; the user's decision: expire keys after a configurable window, one hour by default, documented properly.

**Semantics.** A key is kept for *at least* `idempotency_key_retention` after it was recorded, then deleted; a submission bearing it afterwards is processed as new. The Command and its events are untouched - only the memory of the key goes. "At least" rather than exactly: lookups don't filter by age. Only the cleanup removes rows. Filtering lookups would have meant threading the retention through every submission path (REST, GraphQL, the batcher, routes, deadlines, redrives) for no practical gain, since an hour-plus-a-minute is still "about an hour".

**Mechanism.**
- `SkiljBuilder::idempotency_key_retention(Duration)` (default `DEFAULT_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_RETENTION`, one hour) and `keep_idempotency_keys_forever()` (the old behaviour; no task is spawned).
- A background task, like the others (`contain_panic` per bounded context, `skilj.background_task.*` metrics under `task = "idempotency_key_retention"`), runs every minute - or every `retention` if shorter, at least a second apart. It calls `db::delete_expired_idempotency_keys(pool, bc, now - retention, 10_000)` until a batch comes back short. The batch is a `ctid`-subselect `DELETE ... LIMIT`, so no statement locks an unbounded number of rows.
- Index `idempotency_keys_created_at`, created with the table (`ensure_idempotency_keys_table`, now a `raw_sql` batch) on provisioning and every startup. On a large existing table, that first startup builds the index with a plain `CREATE INDEX` (not `CONCURRENTLY` - it runs in the same batch/transaction as the table DDL), briefly blocking writes to that table while it builds. It's a one-time cost, the same register as §37's migration.
- The task sweeps every bounded context in the database, so instances sharing one database with different retentions are effectively governed by the shortest.

**What the window must cover** (documented on the builder method, in the CHANGELOG, the Temporal integration doc and skill): anything that may retry the same key. That means a client or Temporal activity retrying a request it never heard back from; a bridge re-reading old broker messages (a consumer-group reset); a `CrossContextRoute` retry policy retrying one delivery past the window; and `retryParkedDelivery`, whose redrive runs under the original attempt's key precisely so an attempt that committed but reported failure isn't applied twice (§64) - an operator redriving after the window loses that protection. External-message watermarks (§39) do *not* expire: one number per partition doesn't grow with traffic, and forgetting one would re-admit every redelivery.

**Spec.** `config.idempotency_key_retention: Duration = 1.hour`. `ProcessCommand`'s "Nothing expires" paragraph now describes the window and the deployment's obligation. The watermark paragraph no longer leans on "the same treatment a recorded idempotency key gets". `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged.

Found while editing and fixed in a follow-up: the same `ProcessCommand` prose still said a key is "deliberately not scoped to the calling identity" (answering two callers with the same key as one, and sharing one record across the GraphQL and REST tracks), and `recorded_acceptance(command_type, idempotency_key)` had no caller argument - both stale since §37 made keys `client_id`-scoped. The black box is now `recorded_acceptance(command_type, client_id, idempotency_key)`, the scoping paragraph states why the caller is part of the key (unrelated callers routinely pick the same business-derived key; `client_id` comes from authentication, so no caller can place a key under another's identity) and what that gives up (the tracks don't share records; a retry deduplicates only under the credential the original used). Both `DuplicateAcceptanceReturnsTheOriginalOutcome` guarantees now say "by the same Role" / "with the same CommandToken", and `CommandTrigger`'s "the same one, literally" paragraph now says the mechanism is shared, not the records. Prose and a black-box argument only; `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged.

Tests: `a_key_deduplicates_within_its_retention_and_is_new_after_it` (`skilj/tests/idempotency_key_retention.rs`, its own binary because the task sweeps the whole database; retention 1 s: a retry within the window is deduplicated, the key is then deleted, and the same key afterwards is a new command with new events) and `expired_idempotency_keys_are_deleted_in_bounded_batches` (`skilj-core/tests/persistence.rs`: rows older than the cutoff go 2, then 1, then 0 per call with a batch of 2; a newer row stays).

<a id="wait-for-sequence-expensive"></a>
## 88. `waitForSequence` can't be used to make a query expensive

`ProjectionQuery`'s read-your-writes wait (`wait_until_caught_up`) polled `db::get_projection` - three queries: the bounded context, the projection row, its consumed event types - every 20 ms until the projection's `caught_up_to` reached `waitForSequence` or `projection_query_wait_timeout` (default 5 s) ran out. That's about 250 lookups, 750 queries, for a query that waits the whole time. `waitForSequence` is caller-controlled and wasn't checked against anything. So any reader could name a sequence that will never be reached and make every `projection` field cost the full timeout's worth of polling - ten per request under §72's expensive-field budget - while holding the request open for the whole wait.

The spec already defines what the argument is: "the highest `Event.sequence` already known", typically from the triggered events of a command the caller just submitted. A known sequence is a committed one. So:

- **Refuse what can't be known.** A `waitForSequence` above the bounded context's latest committed sequence (`db::latest_sequence`, one `MAX` over the primary key) is refused before any waiting with `wait_for_sequence_not_committed`. It's distinct from `projection_caught_up_timed_out` on purpose: a timeout says "retry", this says the value itself is wrong. A caller can't have learned a sequence before its event committed, so no legitimate use is lost. The one observable difference is a guessed future sequence that some other writer happens to commit during the wait, which used to succeed.
- **Cheaper legitimate waits.** Each poll reads one column (`db::projection_caught_up_to`, one query), and the interval backs off from 20 ms, doubling to 250 ms, capped at the deadline. The first checks stay quick - an async projection's next tick is usually imminent - and a wait that runs the full 5 s now takes about 25 reads instead of about 250 three-query lookups.
- `projectionUpdates` goes through the same path with a delivered event's (committed) sequence, so it only gains the cheaper poll.

Spec: `QueryProjection` gains `requires: wait_for_sequence = null or wait_for_sequence < <events in the bounded context>.count`, before the wait, and its guidance says the refusal is distinguishable from the timeout. `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged.

Tests (`skilj/tests/projection_query.rs`, `projection_query_end_to_end`): the timeout path needs a committed sequence the projection hasn't reached. That can't happen with the file's sync projections, so a new async `LaggingBalance` in a `Skilj` with an hour-long poll interval provides one: waiting for the committed first sequence times out (`projection_caught_up_timed_out`, after at least the 150 ms timeout). The old case - a sequence 1000 past anything committed - is now `wait_for_sequence_not_committed`, answered in under the timeout. With the refusal disabled, it's the timeout again and the test fails.

<a id="event-cache-holes"></a>
## 89. The event cache never serves a hole or a duplicate

`EventCache` keeps each bounded context's most recent events in a window, which `freshen` checks against Postgres on every read. If the window's highest sequence equals `MAX(sequence)`, the window is trusted as complete from its first event on. Otherwise the missing range is loaded. The window was fed from two places, and neither checked what it was adding:

- **`append`** - the post-commit hook every local write path calls - pushed the event unconditionally. Commits don't reach it in sequence order. Another instance's commit never reaches this cache at all, and two concurrent local commits run their post-commit steps in either order. So with a window ending at 10, another instance committing 11, and this one committing and appending 12, the window was `[..10, 12]`. Its highest sequence matched the database's, so `freshen` trusted it, and a read after 10 was served `[12]`. Event 11 was silently skipped. For `GET /v1/events/consume` that's permanent: the cursor moves past it. The same hole reached `GET /v1/events`, `queryEvents`, `countEvents` and the `CrossContextRoute`/deadline catch-up ticks - everything cache-served. A single instance under concurrent writes could do it too, the late append then also leaving the window out of order.
- **`freshen`'s delta** pushed everything after the `known` sequence it had read. A local `append` of the same event landing between its commit and a concurrent read's freshen - or two concurrent freshens - held that event twice, and reads returned it twice.

Fix, in `ContextWindow` itself so no caller can get it wrong:
- `append_committed` (local commits) only extends the window contiguously: exactly `highest + 1`, or anything into an empty window, which vouches for nothing before its first event. At or below `highest` it's already there. Further ahead, there's an unseen event in between, so it's dropped, and the next read's `freshen` loads the range from Postgres, where it's complete. Dropping is always safe; claiming completeness is what wasn't.
- `push_from_database` (a `freshen` delta, complete for its range by construction) accepts anything above `highest` and skips what's already present.

Sequence allocation is gapless per bounded context (the `sequence` row's `UPDATE` rolls back with its transaction), so contiguity is the right test for local appends. And since only local appends are held to it, even a gap in the database would just mean falling back to `freshen`, not a stuck window. No spec change: `LatestEventsAlwaysAvailable` already required this.

Tests (`skilj-core/tests/event_cache.rs`): `appending_past_an_unseen_event_does_not_leave_a_hole` (another writer's event, then a local append past it: served `[b, a]`; before, `[a]`) and `a_late_append_of_an_already_freshened_event_is_not_a_duplicate` (freshen, then the committing path's append: served once; before, twice).

<a id="live-subscription-ordering"></a>
## 90. Live subscriptions deliver in sequence order

`DeliveryIsAtMostOnce` promises that while the connection is live "every matching event arrives once, in sequence order: no duplicates, no gaps". The live feed is the `EventBroadcaster`, which carries events in the order they were *published* on this instance, and that isn't commit order:

- Two concurrent local commits each publish in their own post-commit step, in either order.
- Another instance's event reaches this broadcaster only when its `NOTIFY` arrives and the listener has refetched it (§83). An event this instance commits *after* it is usually published here first. That's routine in any multi-instance deployment, not an edge case.

A subscriber therefore saw 13 before 12, or 12 never (if its `NOTIFY` was lost). A client tracking "the last sequence I received" for the §84 resume handoff resumed from the wrong place.

The same property the event cache relies on (§89) makes this cheap to fix without buffering or timers: within a bounded context, commits happen in sequence order (the sequence row's lock is held until commit, `SequenceIsGaplessPerBoundedContext`). So when event N is visible, every sequence below N is committed. `in_sequence_order` tracks `processed_up_to` - the highest sequence of the subscription's bounded context it has handled, delivered or filtered out, starting from where §84's resume span left off. On an event past `processed_up_to + 1`, it loads the missing range from Postgres (`list_events_for_bounded_context_from_limited`) and hands it to `deliver_one` first, in order. An event at or below `processed_up_to` - a late arrival already loaded that way, or one the resume span covered - is dropped. A jump over more than `max_events_per_read` ends the stream with `subscription_lagged` rather than loading an unbounded range, like a real lag.

A side effect: an event whose `NOTIFY` was lost is now also recovered as soon as any later event of its bounded context arrives. §83's resync still covers a quiet bounded context, where no later event would come.

Cost: one bounded read per subscription per out-of-order arrival - in a multi-instance deployment, roughly each time instances' writes interleave. No spec change; the guarantee already required this. `projectionUpdates` is unaffected: it pushes current state, and order doesn't change that.

Test: `a_live_subscription_delivers_in_sequence_order_across_an_unpublished_event` (`skilj/tests/event_subscription.rs`): an event committed straight to Postgres and never published (standing in for another instance's, or a not-yet-published concurrent commit), then one committed through `submitCommand`. The subscriber receives both, in order, and nothing else. Without the gap fill it only ever receives the second.

<a id="forget-subject-parked-deliveries"></a>
## 91. `forgetSubject` also erases parked deliveries

Crypto-shredding works because every stored copy of a sensitive value is ciphertext under the subject's data key. Events and commands are encrypted at write, and projection and snapshot state is folded from ciphertext and only decrypted on read (`render_event` is the only decryption on a read path; no fold, decider or stored state ever sees plaintext). Destroying the key makes all of it unreadable. `parked_deliveries` (§47, Rust-only - not in the spec) broke that. A parked row's `request_json` is the request as submitted, before any encryption: a bridge's `POST /v1/events/external` or `/v1/commands/trigger` body, or a `CrossContextRoute`'s target command payload. After `forgetSubject`:

- any admin could still read the subject's sensitive values through `parkedDeliveries`;
- `retryParkedDelivery` re-submitted them, and the write path encrypted them under a *new* active key for the same subject - the forgotten data came back, readable.

Fix, with the user's choice of deleting over redacting (a parked row that names a forgotten subject can never legitimately be redriven, so keeping it for triage would only keep a copy): `db::delete_parked_deliveries_for_subject` runs inside `forgetSubject`. It pages through the bounded context's parked rows (§86's deletion-safe cursor) and deletes each one whose request references the subject. A row always lives in the bounded context whose types and keys it would use (the token's for bridge rows, the route's target for route rows), so one context is enough. A row references the subject when the payload its redrive would submit - `request.payload`, or the whole request for route rows - names it through the target type's own sensitive fields. That's `sensitive_field_subjects`, the same derivation encryption uses, so the match is exactly "the subjects this payload would be encrypted under". The target type comes from the row's `ExternalEventToken` or `CommandToken`, or the route's target command type. A row whose type can't be resolved (its token or target context gone) or whose request isn't the redrive's shape can't be redriven anyway, and it's deleted if the subject value appears anywhere in its request, erring toward erasure.

It runs *before* the key is destroyed. If it failed afterwards, `forgetSubject` couldn't be retried - the key is no longer active, so a second call is `EncryptionKey_not_found` - and the plaintext would stay for good. A delivery parked after the erasure is new data about the subject, the same as a new event would be.

Checked for other plaintext copies: idempotency keys store only sequences, external-message cursors only positions, and no log line writes a payload value.

Test: `subject_erasure_end_to_end` (`skilj/tests/subject_erasure.rs`) now parks three `ExternalEvent` rows before `forgetSubject` for subject `user/42`: one naming 42 through `AccountOpened`'s sensitive field, one naming 43, and one whose token doesn't exist but whose request mentions 42. Afterwards only 43's row remains. Without the cleanup, all three do.

<a id="scoped-admin-scope-escape"></a>
## 92. A scoped admin can't mint or revoke its way out of its scope

A `RoleAccessMapping.scope` confines a grant to one owner's records wherever an owner dimension is declared (§23/§25/§30), for admin-level grants too: `inspectSnapshot` is admin-gated and fails closed on a scope mismatch. But the four token-minting rules took a token's `scope` "independent of the minting admin's", and checked the grant only for level and bounded context. So a tenant-scoped admin could mint an `EventReadToken` with no scope and read every owner's events over REST, or a `CommandToken`/`ExternalEventToken`/`DirectCreationToken` with another owner's scope and act as them. Likewise `RevokeToken` let it revoke any token in the bounded context, cutting off other owners' and staff credentials. The spec's own motivating example was only the narrowing case: an unscoped staff admin minting a company-scoped token.

Fix, with the user's choice of confining scoped minters over forbidding scoped admin grants or documenting the escape:

- **Minting** (`scope_for_minted_token`, used by all four `create_*_token` functions): an unscoped grant mints whatever scope it names, unchanged. A scoped grant may name its own scope or none - and then the token *inherits* the grant's scope rather than coming out unrestricted. Naming any other scope is refused with `token_scope_beyond_grant`.
- **Revoking** (`revoke_token`): a scoped grant may revoke only a token whose own scope equals the grant's. Another owner's token, or an unrestricted one, is refused with the same code. `AccessToken::owner_scope` reads the variant's `scope`, separate from the existing `AccessToken::scope`, which is `RevokeToken`'s bounded-context `token_scope`.

Spec: the four minting rules gain `requires: access_mapping.scope = null or scope = null or scope = access_mapping.scope` and stamp `minted_scope = scope ?? access_mapping.scope`. `RevokeToken` gains `requires: access_mapping.scope = null or token.scope = access_mapping.scope` (`scope` is declared on all four variants). `CreateEventReadToken`'s note, which states the reasoning for all four, now distinguishes unscoped minters (free, narrowing is ordinary) from scoped ones (confined). `allium check`/`analyse` unchanged.

Not changed, and worth knowing: other admin surfaces stay bounded-context-wide for a scoped admin, because they aren't per-owner by nature. That covers type registration, `parkedDeliveries` (whose rows carry no owner), and `forgetSubject` (keyed by subject, not owner). A deployment that needs an admin fully confined to one tenant should give that tenant its own bounded context.

Tests (`skilj-core/tests/token_lifecycle.rs`): `an_unscoped_admin_mints_any_scope`, `a_scoped_admin_mints_only_within_its_own_scope` (all four kinds: omitted inherits, the same scope passes, another is `token_scope_beyond_grant`) and `a_scoped_admin_revokes_only_within_its_own_scope` (own scope revoked; another owner's or an unrestricted token refused; an unscoped admin revokes any).

<a id="database-error-logging"></a>
## 93. Database error text stays in the server log

`skilj_core::Error::message()` - what both renderers put in a response's `message` - returned `sqlx::Error::to_string()` for `Database` and `MigrateError::to_string()` for `Migration`. So a 500 answered with Postgres' own text: `relation "bc_acme_corp.events" does not exist`, `duplicate key value violates unique constraint ...`. That names schemas (every bounded context's schema is `bc_<name>`, and bounded contexts are often tenants), constraints, columns and SQL fragments. The `database_error` code already told the caller everything actionable. This also reached callers before authentication completed (REST token resolution is a database read), and `BatchFailed` copied the leader's message to every follower.

Fix:
- `message()` is generic for both: "an internal database error occurred" / "... migration error ...". Two cases keep their own wording because it's useful and reveals nothing: `RowNotFound` ("a record this request needed no longer exists", the outcome the hard-delete panic sweeps turned stale references into) and `PoolTimedOut` ("... all busy - retry shortly"). Codes are unchanged. `BatchFailed` followers inherit the generic text through `Error::batch_failed`.
- New `SkiljRejection::internal_detail()` (default `None`; `Some(raw text)` for these two) carries the cause. `skilj-rest`'s `IntoResponse` and `skilj-graphql`'s `to_graphql_error` log it at `error`, with the code, inside the request's span. So the `trace_id`/`traceId` every error response already carries leads an operator straight to it. Business and access rejections are untouched: their messages are written for the caller.

Checked: no resolver or route builds a caller-facing message from an internal error's `to_string()` outside these two renderers. The one `to_string()` left (`InvalidParkedDeliveryRequest`) is a decode error about the caller's own request body.

Tests: `a_database_error_does_not_reach_the_caller_verbatim` in both `skilj-rest` (the full `IntoResponse` body: code `database_error`, the generic message, no schema name anywhere) and `skilj-graphql` (`to_graphql_error`'s message), plus `a_vanished_row_and_pool_exhaustion_stay_distinguishable` (and that `internal_detail` still has the raw text). `skilj-graphql` gains `sqlx` as a dev-dependency only, to build such an error; the library itself stays free of it.

<a id="key-retention-startup"></a>
## 94. Key retention waits out startup

§87's retention counts wall-clock time from when a key was recorded, and every instance swept from the moment it started. Several recovery paths retry under a key right after a restart: a `'firing'` deadline reclaimed after its 5-minute stale window (`fire_due_deadlines` resubmits under `skilj-deadline:{id}`), a `CrossContextRoute` re-reading a source event whose cursor update didn't land, and a bridge whose broker redelivers a message whose offset or acknowledgement wasn't committed. Each exists for a crash between a command committing and the bookkeeping after it. If the whole deployment then stayed down longer than the retention, the restarted instances ran the sweep and those recovery paths at the same moment, and the sweep could delete the key first - the recovered delivery then landed as a second command. Found while checking deadline firing's multi-instance safety, which is itself sound: the claim is a conditional `UPDATE`, and only its winner submits.

Fix: an instance waits `min(retention, 1 hour)` (`IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_STARTUP_GRACE`) before its first sweep. The recovery paths all run at startup and finish within minutes, so they find their keys. Capping the grace at an hour keeps a deployment that restarts more often than a long retention from never sweeping. In a rolling deploy the other instances keep sweeping - only a whole-deployment outage delays cleanup - and the cost is at most an hour's more keys after a restart. The spec's "kept for at least the retention" is unchanged; this only ever keeps keys longer.

Test: `a_key_deduplicates_within_its_retention_and_is_new_after_it` (`skilj/tests/idempotency_key_retention.rs`, retention 2 s) now inserts a key recorded two hours earlier before `build()`. It's still there half a second after startup, and gone once the grace has passed, along with the test's own keys. With the grace removed, the first sweep deletes it immediately and the test fails.

<a id="event-cache-lifecycle"></a>
## 95. The event cache can't outlive the bounded context it cached

`DeleteBoundedContext` hard-deletes a context's schema and "frees the name for reuse" (`hard_delete_bounded_context`). The event cache keys its windows by bounded-context *name* and has no eviction at all. Even an instance that evicted on delete couldn't cover the others, since deletion isn't pushed to them. `freshen` decided a window's validity from sequences alone, and a successor's sequences are indistinguishable from its predecessor's: both start at 0. Reproduced: a context with three cached events is deleted and recreated under the same name with one new event, and the cache serves the three deleted events. Once the successor's sequence passes the old window's highest, the delta read appends its events onto the dead ones. Every cache-backed read serves that window - `GET /v1/events`, consume, untagged `queryEvents`, `countEvents`, the command path's DCB pre-check, and the route/deadline catch-ups - so a new tenant given a deleted tenant's name would be shown the deleted tenant's events, on every instance that had them cached.

Fix: each `ContextWindow` records `table` - the OID of the `bc_<name>.events` table its events came from. A recreated context gets a new table and so a new OID, on every instance, with no coordination. `freshen` reads it with the latest sequence in one query (`db::events_table_identity`: `'bc_x.events'::regclass::oid` alongside `MAX(sequence)`), so it costs no extra round trip, and refills the window wholesale on a mismatch. A window only `append` has started (no stamp, since a local commit doesn't know the table) is refilled on its first read for the same reason. `warm` and every refill stamp the OID read *before* loading the events. A delete-and-recreate racing a refill then leaves a stale stamp that the next `freshen` corrects, never a fresh stamp on old events.

Checked, and not affected: live subscriptions on the deleted context (`subscription_selects` compares the whole `BoundedContext`, `created_at` included, and the grant re-check fails because deletion cascades the grants); the GraphQL schema and template cache (rebuilt on the `RegistrationChanged` notification that creation already sends); and the command batcher's per-name queues (transient).
