It is a resilience setting, so the user decided: off by default. `skilj::default_pool_options()` is sqlx's defaults with `test_before_acquire(false)`, and `build()` uses it when `pool_options(...)` isn't called. Options passed to `pool_options` are used as given, so its documentation says to start from `default_pool_options()` to keep the setting. What is given up: a connection that breaks while idle in the pool (a database restart or failover, a dropped network path) fails the first statement sent on it instead of being replaced first, which is at most one failed request per pooled connection after a restart. The ping sqlx sends when a connection is given back still runs, so a connection that broke while in use never returns to the pool. The benchmark follows the default; `SKILJ_BENCH_TEST_BEFORE_ACQUIRE=true` turns the ping back on.

<a id="chunked-snapshot-catch-up"></a>
## 197. Snapshot catch-up folds a chunk of events per transaction

skilj-helpdesk's create-ticket latency report (2026-10-09) found the limit after its `CompanySnapshot` fix in skilj: snapshot catch-up still locked, folded and rewrote a row once per event, about 50 events/s on that machine. At ~100 commands/s the snapshot fell behind, so every `decide_from_snapshot` read a growing "events since". The projection report from the same day found the same thing for `CompanyActiveTickets`, a partitioned async projection: §182 batched the unpartitioned path and listed the partitioned one under "Not changed".

**What it did.**
- `catch_up_snapshots`, unpartitioned, used one transaction per event. In it, per snapshot, it ran `get_or_create_snapshot_state_for_update` (a get-or-create-with-lock that also resets a row at an older `Snapshot::VERSION`), folded, ran an `UPDATE`, and upserted `snapshot_progress`.
- `catch_up_partitioned_snapshot` used one transaction per partition per tick, with the same two statements per event inside it.
- For a row at `as_of_sequence = -1`, just created or reset, `fold_snapshot_tag_history` (§152) read that tag value's history through the tag index, one value at a time.
- `catch_up_partitioned_projection` used one transaction per partition per tick, and a get-or-create-with-lock and an `UPDATE` per key per event inside it.

**Change.** `fold_snapshot_chunk_in_tx` folds a run of events into one snapshot, on the caller's transaction:
1. It locks or creates every tag value the events touch, in one `INSERT ... SELECT unnest(...) ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING`, sorted by value. The version reset is the same `CASE` as before, in the same statement.
2. A row at -1 is refolded from the default state over its tag value's history, through its last event in the run (`refold_snapshot_histories`). That is what folding the history at its first event and then each later event did. One paged read (`tags @> ANY(...)`, 1000 a page) covers every such row at once.
3. The other events are folded in memory, keeping the `as_of_sequence` guard per row (Codeberg #25).
4. Every row is written back with one `UPDATE ... FROM unnest(...)`. A row's owner is the last owner tag a folded event carried; a row no event gave one keeps the stored one (`COALESCE`).

The unpartitioned path calls it through `fold_snapshots_chunk` for chunks of `CATCH_UP_EVENTS_PER_TRANSACTION` (100) events, once per snapshot (in name order), then moves each snapshot's progress to the chunk's end and commits. The partitioned path calls it once per partition transaction, with that partition's values only.

`catch_up_partitioned_projection` now does what §182 does, inside its existing transaction: it collects the keys its partition's events touch, locks them in one statement in sorted order, folds in memory and writes them back in one statement. The lock, fold and write statements are now shared with the unpartitioned chunk: `lock_chunk_states`, `fold_into_chunk_states`, `write_chunk_states`. `get_or_create_snapshot_state_for_update` and `fold_snapshot_tag_history` are gone.

**Why it's the same.** Each row is locked before it is read and kept locked until commit, so checking `as_of_sequence` once is checking it every time. A row refolded through its last event in the run holds exactly the events it held before: its tag's events are the history read's events, in the same order. Partitioned transactions were already all or nothing. Sorting the values is new. Two instances on the unpartitioned path, which has no advisory lock, now lock a chunk's rows in the same order.

**A failing event.** As in §182, a failed chunk reports how many of its events came before the failing one. `catch_up_snapshots` folds those again in a transaction of their own, commits, and returns the error. A refold that fails is blamed on the first of the row's events in the chunk at or after the failing event: that is where the per-event loop would have reached it. The first version blamed the row's first event instead, and `a_failing_event_mid_chunk_keeps_the_progress_before_it` caught it: the row came back empty. History from before the chunk is blamed on the row's first event.

**Measured.** `skilj-core/tests/snapshot_catch_up_throughput.rs` (new, `#[ignore]`d) commits 5000 events, then times back-to-back `catch_up_snapshots` calls until the snapshot has caught up. **one** is one tag value for every event, **per-account** 500 values, **partitioned** the same with `PARTITION_COUNT` 4, and **reset** a caught-up per-account snapshot whose `VERSION` was bumped, walking 5000 more events, so every row is refolded from 10 earlier events. `projection_catch_up_throughput.rs` gains **partitioned**, per-account with `PARTITION_COUNT` 4. Embedded Postgres, release build, alternating a worktree of the commit before with this one, each with its own target directory (§196):

| scenario | before | after | refolding through `event_tags` (§198) |
|---|---|---|---|
| snapshot, one | 1,570-1,720 events/s | 59,000-85,000 | 74,000-79,000 |
| snapshot, per-account | 990-1,050 | 31,000-33,000 | 41,000-45,000 |
| snapshot, partitioned | 1,600-1,650 | 24,000-26,000 | 52,000-53,000 |
| snapshot, reset | 740-760 | 6,600-6,800 | 37,000-38,000 |
| projection, partitioned | 3,700-4,300 | 49,000-53,000 | |

The last column is after §198, which moved the history read of `refold_snapshot_histories` from the GIN index on `events.tags` to `event_tags`: a new tag value's first refold takes that read too, which is why every scenario but **one** gains.

The unpartitioned projection scenarios didn't change (`total` 60,000-67,000, `per-account` 33,000-36,000, `both` 15,000-17,000, before and after). The partitioned snapshot is slower than per-account because it takes four transactions, one per partition, for each 1000-event tick. A reset refolds 10 events of history for each of the 500 rows. All four snapshot scenarios now take one transaction per chunk where they took one per event, so on the helpdesk's disk, where each commit costs a 2.2 ms fsync, the gain should be larger still.

**Tests.** `a_chunked_catch_up_folds_every_event_once_across_chunks` (`skilj-core/tests/snapshot_context.rs`): 250 events over seven accounts, three of them already held, in one tick of three chunks. Every row ends with each of its events folded once, at its last event. `a_failing_event_mid_chunk_keeps_the_progress_before_it`: a fold failing on the fourth event leaves the first three committed. The existing §152 version-bump tests, the partition tests and the owner tests pass unchanged, through the new code.

**Not changed.** `fold_history_into_new_sync_projection` still commits once per event; it runs once per registration.

<a id="consistency-query"></a>
## 198. A command's consistency query: types, tags and latest-only

skilj-helpdesk's create-ticket latency report (2026-10-09) traced its throughput decay to `CreateTicket` reading its company's whole history under the bounded context's lock. A command could only declare tags, and `matching_events` was every event carrying any of them. `TicketCreated` carries the company's tag (projections scope rows by it), so every new ticket replayed every ticket the company had filed. The helpdesk worked around it with a `CompanySnapshot`, which needs a catch-up (§197) and still reads the events since. What `CreateTicket` needs is two facts: the company's latest lifecycle event, and whether a `TicketCreated` used its ticket id.

**The model.** DCB's query (dcb.events): a list of items, OR'd. An item names event types (any type when it names none) and tags, all of which an event must carry, AND'd, as the user chose. skilj adds `latest` per item, a count: of the item's matches, only that many, the ones with the highest sequences; unset, every match. `latest()` is `last(1)`, what a status needs. The user asked for a count rather than only "the latest" so a decision that needs the last few events - at most three open tickets per requester, the last five failed logins - is a bounded read too. Per item rather than per type: an item over four lifecycle types with `latest()` gives the latest of the four; per type is one item per type.

- `QueryItemMapping { event_types, tag_mappings, latest: Option<u32> }` (`skilj_core::shared`), declared by `CommandType::consistency_query()` with a small builder (`QueryItemMapping::types(...).tagged(...).latest()`, or `.last(n)`). Derived per command into `QueryItem { event_types, tags, latest }` by `event_store::derive_query`, as `derive_tags` derives tags.
- Empty, the default, is one item per derived consistency tag, any type, every match (`effective_query`): exactly the old behaviour, including a list-valued tag mapping, which derives several tags of one key and used to match an event carrying any of them.
- `decide()` still gets one flat slice: every selected event, in sequence order, each once (`select_matching_events`). Deciders already branch on the event's type, so nothing about its signature changes.
- The boundary is the highest selected sequence (`query_boundary`).

**The conflict narrows with the read.** Under the lock, an event committed since the read conflicts when it matches any item, whatever its `latest`: it would have been among the item's newest. The decider then runs again over the read plus those events, selected again, so a newer match displaces the oldest an item kept. An event carrying the command's tag but matching no item no longer conflicts. For the helpdesk that is the bigger change: three `CreateTicket`s of one company in one batch used to conflict with any ticket of that company committed after their read, and now only with a lifecycle event of the company or a ticket of their own id. The flip side, stated in the spec: the query has to name every fact `decide()` depends on.

**Where the query lives.** On the compiled command type, read through `CommandDispatcher::consistency_query` (default `None`, so a dispatcher written by hand is unaffected), like `snapshot()` - not registered in `command_types`, as the user chose. The query and `decide()` are written against each other, so they come from the same build; a registered query from a newer instance during a rolling deploy would hand an older `decide()` a set it wasn't written for. The spec says the same: `CommandType.consistency_query` is part of the deployed declaration, not a `RegisterCommandType` parameter, and its rules are the invariant `ConsistencyQueryIsWellFormed`, which `build()` holds (`validate_consistency_queries`): every event type an item names must be registered in the same bounded context by the same builder, every item tag mapping must be one of the command type's `tag_mappings()`, an item must name types or tags, `latest` can't be 0 (it would read nothing yet conflict on every match), and a query can't be combined with `snapshot()`, which folds by one tag and knows nothing of the query. `Command.consistency_tags` is unchanged and is still what owner scoping reads; each command now also records its query in `commands.consistency_query` (empty for the default).

**Reading it.** The default keeps its old path, unchanged. A declared query is one statement (`list_events_matching_query_with_bc`): the events whose sequence is in the `UNION` of one sub-select per item, so one snapshot, which the re-check's starting point needs (§178).
- An item with types and tags reads `event_tags`, a new table of one row per tag per event, `(tag_key, tag_value, event_type_name, sequence)`, indexed in that order, on its first tag and its types; other tags are checked on the event found. An item with `latest` adds `ORDER BY sequence DESC LIMIT $n`. Its cost is the matches of that tag and those types, not every event with the tag: for `CreateTicket` the company's few lifecycle events and the one ticket.
- An item with tags only uses the GIN index on `events.tags`, as tag reads always have. One with types only uses `events_by_type`, and without `latest` reads the type's whole history: the spec says choosing that is the command type author's call.
- The statement's text depends on the query's shape only, so a command type sends the same one to the statement cache (§193).
- The event cache serves a query read from a window holding everything after the read's start, filtering by the query and selecting each counted item's newest matches in memory, and misses otherwise.

The re-check under the lock (§178) for a declared query runs the same statement with every item's `latest` unset, from the read's position. The batch's single re-check (§196) is a tag query over the union of the batch's consistency tags; every item's tags are among them, so each command keeps its part by matching its own query. A command with an item that has no tags isn't covered by that tag query and re-checks on its own.

**`event_tags`, filled by the database.** A statement-level `AFTER INSERT` trigger on `events` (`REFERENCING NEW TABLE`, one `INSERT ... SELECT` per statement, so a batch's multi-row insert pays it once) writes the rows. Not skilj's insert paths: during a rolling deploy an older instance writes events too, knows nothing of the table, and a missing row would be a missed conflict. `ensure_event_tags_index` runs at provisioning and on every `build()`, under an advisory lock like §189's. For a bounded context from before it, it creates the table, backfills it from `events`, creates the index, the function and the trigger, all in one transaction holding `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` on `events`, so reads go on and no event commits between the backfill and the trigger. Every later start finds the table and locks nothing (§158). It also adds `commands.consistency_query` the same gated way. The cost: one row per tag per event, plus its index entry.

**Measured.** `skilj-core/tests/consistency_query_read.rs` (`#[ignore]`d) seeds one company that signed up and filed N tickets, then times the read before the lock for a new ticket (`resolve_command_submission`, event cache off, median of 50), tagged by company alone versus with the `CreateTicket` query. Embedded Postgres, release build:

| tickets | tags: median | events to `decide()` | query: median | events to `decide()` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.93 ms | 101 | 0.59 ms | 1 |
| 1,000 | 3.4 ms | 1,001 | 0.76 ms | 1 |
| 10,000 | 40 ms | 10,001 | 0.75 ms | 1 |
| 50,000 | 189 ms | 50,001 | 0.83 ms | 1 |

The query's read doesn't grow with the company's history; the tag read grows linearly, and its events are then decoded and folded by `decide()` too. The helpdesk's step-4 ramp put `CreateTicket`'s `decide` phase at 49-604 ms per batch, under the lock; with the query it is two index probes and one event, and the re-check under the lock no longer sees the company's other tickets.

**Tests.** `skilj-core/tests/consistency_query.rs`: `decide()` gets the company's latest lifecycle event and none of its tickets, and the command records its query; the latest lifecycle event and a used ticket id decide; between read and lock, another ticket of the company isn't a conflict (one `decide()`) while the company expiring is (decided again with the expiry in place of the sign-up); a batch of three tickets read before another ticket of the company commits accepts all three with three `decide()` calls; `event_tags` is backfilled for a bounded context without it, and kept by the trigger afterwards. `an_item_keeps_its_last_n_matches`: `last(2)` gives the company's two newest tickets, from the cache and from Postgres, and a ticket committed between read and lock is a conflict that displaces the older of the two. `skilj/tests/consistency_query_build.rs`: the five refusals.

**Surfaces.**
- GraphQL `CommandType.consistencyQuery: [QueryItemMapping!]!` (`eventTypes`, `tagMappings`, `latest`), on the admin surface (`commandTypes`), so `@inaccessible` in the federation description like the rest of it; the fixtures were re-recorded and still compose with Apollo's and Hive's composition. It shows the query as the answering instance has the command type compiled: a type registered over GraphQL, or one this instance doesn't deploy, shows `[]`. skilj-inspector and skilj-tui show no command type tags either, so neither shows the query.
- skilj-codegen: `[[command_type.query]]` tables (`event_types`, `tags`, `latest`) generate a `consistency_query()` override. `tags` names keys of the command type's own `tags`, so an item's tag mappings are always among them; `generate()` refuses an item naming an event type the file doesn't declare (the generated event enum couldn't carry it to `decide()` anyway), a tag the command type doesn't map, an item with neither, and `latest = 0`. The override is emitted with `Vec::from([...])`, which prettyplease formats, rather than `vec![...]`, whose tokens it leaves on one line.
- skilj-demo: `OpenCourse` declares `CourseOpened` tagged by course, `.latest()` - it only needs to know whether the course is open, and read every enrollment of it before. `opening_an_open_course_is_refused_through_its_query` (`skilj-demo/tests/courses.rs`).

**The snapshot refold reads `event_tags` too.** §197's `refold_snapshot_histories` read a chunk's reset rows' histories through the GIN index, paging by `ORDER BY sequence LIMIT 1000`. GIN keeps no order, so every page rebuilt and sorted the bitmap of every value's whole history. It now pages through `event_tags`, `tag_key = $1 AND tag_value = ANY($2)` with the sequence bounds and the `LIMIT`. A second index on `(tag_key, tag_value, sequence)` was measured and left out: with 100 values of 500 events each refolded after a `VERSION` bump, GIN took 2.2 s, `event_tags` 0.54 s, and the extra index 0.54 → 0.50 s, not worth a write per tag per event. With 20 values of 5,000 each: 1.1 s, 0.81 s and 0.78 s.

**Not done.** skilj-helpdesk: `CreateTicket` can declare the query and drop `CompanySnapshot` - in that repository.

<a id="before-the-release"></a>
## 199. Checks and fixes before the release

A list of things to improve before releasing the work since 0.0.9; the user chose the "should do" items. This section records them in the order they were done.

**The broker and Temporal suites, run for real.** CI has no Docker, so the Kafka, AMQP, NATS and Temporal suites always skip there. They were run against real services in Docker. The bridges' tests passed unchanged: NATS 11 tests, AMQP 11, Kafka 14. Temporal's skipped anyway, because its tests download Temporal's test server from temporal.download, which the network here blocks. `SKILJ_TEMPORAL_TEST_SERVER` now names a `temporal-test-server` binary to run instead; the Java SDK's GitHub releases publish it. A skip also prints the startup error in full, not just its summary, which would have shown the cause at once. With it, the 8 Temporal tests passed. AGENTS.md says how.

**Fewer round trips before the lock.** §196 left a command at about 13 statements, and the next two biggest costs were reads before the lock:

- *Token resolution* read `access_token_index` to find which bounded context's schema holds the token, then the token's row there. A token never moves to another bounded context, so `fetch_access_token_row` now remembers the location after the first read, up to 10,000 tokens, after which it starts over. Only the location is remembered: the row, with its status and revocation, is read on every request. A remembered location with no row - the token deleted, or its bounded context hard-deleted, which drops the schema (`42P01`) - is forgotten and the index read again, so a stale entry corrects itself. Token ids are random, so a remembered id can't name a different token. Test: `a_remembered_token_location_never_hides_a_revocation_or_a_deletion` (`skilj-core/tests/persistence.rs`).
- *A bounded context's row* was read, then its creating role, then its template and the template's role: up to four round trips on nearly every request, for a bounded context made by a superadmin from a template. `get_bounded_context` now reads all four in one statement through `LEFT JOIN`s (`hydrated_bounded_context_columns`, `HYDRATED_BOUNDED_CONTEXT_FROM`), and `get_command_type` uses the same joins with the command type. This also closes the race a separate template read had, a template deleted between the two reads, since one statement reads one snapshot.

The post-commit `NOTIFY` stays a statement of its own after the commit. Moving it into the transaction would save one round trip per batch, not per command, and would mean `commit_command_batch` reporting which path wrote the batch.

**`_entities` reads a page at once.** A router asks for a page of instances, mostly of one type. Each was resolved like a `projection(...)` call: the projection's registration, the team check and the state row, per instance. The resolver now groups the representations by projection and does each group's grant, registration and team check once. It reads the group's rows in one `key = ANY($2)` statement (`db::get_projection_states_and_owners`), then answers in the router's order. Each instance is still built by the same code as `projection(...)` (`projection_instance`), so defaults, decryption and access checks are unchanged. Test: `entities_resolve_through_the_callers_own_grant` (`skilj/tests/graphql_federation.rs`) now also asks for a repeated key and an instance with no state yet, out of order.

**The federation smoke test, with real routers.** `scripts/federation-smoke.sh` runs skilj-demo behind Apollo Router 2.18, the Apollo Router 3.0 preview and Hive Router 0.3, and passed everything on all three: a mutation, a projection, a request with no credential refused, and `Account.balance` resolved through skilj's `_entities`. The subscription check passed on Hive. On Apollo it skips as designed, because Apollo's router needs GraphOS for subscriptions. The script used to need Rover, which comes from rover.apollo.dev, and that host is blocked here. Rover is now optional. Without it, the script introspects each subgraph with `curl` (`_service { sdl }`) and composes with `@apollo/composition` (`scripts/federation/supergraph.mjs`), the same library Rover uses.

**An end-to-end load run.** `scripts/load-demo.py` drives skilj-demo's REST `DepositMoney` from N clients, either one account per command (`spread`) or one account for all (`hot`). It then checks Postgres: the event sequence has no gap or duplicate, every accepted command has exactly one event with the same amount, and the sync `AccountBalance` projection sums to the same total. It was run in release mode against a local Postgres, directly and through a proxy adding 1 ms per round trip, at 1, 8, 32 and 80 clients. Every check passed and every request got a 200:

| clients | spread, direct | spread, +1 ms | hot, direct | hot, +1 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 240/s, p50 4 ms | 36/s, p50 27 ms | 31-170/s | 19/s |
| 8 | 550/s, p50 14 ms | 177/s, p50 44 ms | 36-195/s | 39/s |
| 32 | 610-1020/s, p50 30-51 ms | 212/s, p50 151 ms | 41/s | 49/s |
| 80 | 446/s, p50 172 ms | 223/s, p50 358 ms | 42/s | 54/s |

Spread throughput levels off around 32 clients. Past that point extra clients only queue for the sequence lock, which the slow-statement log confirms is the only wait. The hot rows depend on how long the run is, not on the number of clients. `DepositMoney` tags on its account, so every command reads that account's whole history before deciding: a fresh account takes about 6 ms a command, one with a few thousand deposits 30 ms or more. That is DCB without a snapshot, as designed. The demo shows the snapshot path with `WithdrawMoneyFast`.

The run found one real problem. The background snapshot worker (`catch_up_snapshots`) handles each event in its own transaction, in 9 statements when the tag value is new: begin, the row, the tag's history with its event types, origin commands and command types, the update, the progress row, and commit. Through the 1 ms proxy it folded about 36 events a second while the server wrote about 220, so the backlog kept growing for as long as the load lasted. Commands stay correct, because `resolve_snapshot_context` folds whatever comes after a snapshot's `as_of_sequence`, but a snapshot-backed command gets slower the further the worker falls behind.
